steps.body:
In Algebra 1 you were HANDED exponential growth as a fact: some things grow like bˣ, and that is that.

Here is where it comes from.

**dy/dt = ky** — *the rate of growth is proportional to how much you already have.*

Separate and integrate: (1/y)dy = k dt → ln|y| = kt + C → **y = y₀e^(kt)**.

Exponential growth is not a species of function. It is what dy/dt = ky *forces*.

explanationVariants: "The more there is, the faster it grows" is exactly dy/dt = ky: the rate is proportional to the amount.
Bacteria divide, so twice as many bacteria produce twice as many new ones. That single sentence IS the differential equation.

widget.prompt: A bacterial colony grows at a rate proportional to its size. Which equation says that?

options.label: dP/dt = kP
options.feedback: Right — and everything else follows. Twice as many bacteria means twice as many divisions per second, which is precisely proportionality.

options.label: dP/dt = k
options.feedback: That says it grows at a CONSTANT rate, however big it is — which would give a straight line, not exponential growth.

options.label: dP/dt = kt
options.feedback: That says the growth rate depends on the CLOCK, not on the population. A colony does not check the time before dividing.

options.label: P = ekt
options.feedback: That is (nearly) the SOLUTION. The question asks for the differential equation — the sentence about rates that produces it.

widget.prompt: dy/dt = 0.5y. Drag the starting value to 2, and look at what the field does as you move UP the page.
widget.successFeedback: The segments get steeper the higher you go — that IS 'the more there is, the faster it grows', drawn. And every curve is a scaled copy of every other: doubling the starting value doubles the whole curve, because y₀ is a MULTIPLIER in y = y₀e^(kt), not an addition.
widget.lowFeedback: Below 2 — a smaller starting amount, and (look) a flatter curve, because there is less to breed from.
widget.highFeedback: Above 2 — a bigger starting amount, and a steeper curve from the very first instant.

cml.actionGoal: Change an initial condition and trace a solution that remains tangent to the local direction field.

predict.prompt: dy/dt = 0.5y. Move straight up the page — same t, larger y. The slope marks there will be…

options.label: The same — t has not changed

predict.reveal: Steeper, and by exactly the same factor the height grew. "Rate proportional to amount" is not a description of exponential growth — it is the instruction that produces it, and the field shows the instruction being obeyed at every height.

explanationVariants: Note the exponent is kt = 1 at t = 10, which is why the answer is exactly 200e.

widget.prompt: A colony has dP/dt = 0.1P and P(0) = 200. Find P(10), to one decimal.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the starting population. In 10 hours it has grown by a factor of e^(0.1×10) = e ≈ 2.718.
That would be 200 × 10 — LINEAR growth. Exponential growth multiplies by e^(kt), not by t.
That looks like 10% growth once. Exponential growth compounds continuously: 200e ≈ 543.7.

steps.body:
Make k **negative** and the same equation becomes decay:

**dy/dt = −ky** → y = y₀e^(−kt)

Radioactive atoms, cooling coffee, drugs leaving the bloodstream — all obey *the rate of loss is proportional to what is left*. And the **half-life** is the time to fall by half:

y₀/2 = y₀e^(−kT) → **T = ln2 / k**

One equation, two behaviours, and the sign of k decides which.

explanationVariants: The half-life does not depend on how much you started with — which is the strange and useful fact about exponential decay.

widget.prompt: A substance has a half-life of 5 days. Find its decay constant k, to four decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the HALF-LIFE itself. The constant is k = ln2/5 ≈ 0.1386.
That is 1/5. The relationship carries a logarithm: k = ln2/T ≈ 0.6931/5.
That is ln 2. You must still divide by the half-life, 5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: T = ln2/k → k = ln2/5 ≈ 0.1386 per day.

steps.body: Time two halvings against each other.

widget.prompt: dy/dt = −0.5y. Drag the starting value to 6, then back down to 2, and each time follow the curve until it has fallen to HALF of where it began.
widget.successFeedback: The run from 6 down to 3 takes the same stretch of t as the run from 2 down to 1. The fall out of 6 is far steeper in absolute terms, but there is proportionally more to lose, and the two effects cancel exactly.
widget.lowFeedback: Below 6 — a smaller start and a gentler fall. Take it up to 6 first; the comparison this step asks for needs a large start and a small one.
widget.highFeedback: Above 6 — larger still. Come back to 6, then drop to 2 and follow each curve down to half its own starting height.

hints: Write the decay: y = y₀e^(−kt), and ask when y = y₀/2.
y₀/2 = y₀e^(−kT) — the y₀ CANCELS from both sides.
So T = ln2/k, and it does not mention y₀ at all.
explanationVariants: The y₀ cancels, so the half-life is the same whether you start with a kilogram or a microgram: T = ln2/k.
That is why 'half-life' is a property of the SUBSTANCE and not of the sample — a fact that would be hard to believe if you had not just watched it fall out of the algebra.

widget.prompt: Two samples of the same substance start with 1 kg and 1 microgram. Which halves faster?

options.label: Neither; the same k gives both samples the same half-life.
options.feedback: Right, and it is why half-life is a property of the SUBSTANCE, not of the sample. The kilogram loses vastly more mass per second, but it takes the same time to lose half of itself.

options.label: Kilogram sample; more mass makes its half-life shorter.
options.feedback: It loses more MASS per second, certainly. But it also has more to lose, and the two effects cancel exactly: the fraction lost per second is the same.

options.label: Microgram sample; less mass makes its half-life shorter.
options.feedback: It also decays proportionally more slowly in absolute terms. The PROPORTION lost per second is identical, which is what a half-life measures.

options.label: Both depend on k, so their half-lives cannot be compared.
options.feedback: k is a property of the substance and is the SAME for both samples. What the question asks is whether the starting amount matters — and it does not.

steps.body: The equation that explains the function.
takeaways: dy/dt = ky — the rate is proportional to the amount — FORCES y = y₀e^(kt). Exponential growth is not a species of curve; it is what that sentence implies.
Negative k gives decay, and the half-life T = ln2/k does not depend on how much you started with.
Algebra 1 handed you bˣ as a fact. This is where it comes from.
steps.teaser: Next: what happens when the growth rate stops being constant.

concept.body: Read the sentence, then write the equation. *'Grows in proportion to how much there is'* is dy/dt = ky. Separate it, integrate it, and out comes y = y₀e^(kt) — every time.

explanationVariants: 'The rate of loss is proportional to what remains' is dy/dt = −ky, with the minus sign carrying the word 'loss'.
Proportional to the amount means the amount appears on the right-hand side.

widget.prompt: 'A drug leaves the blood at a rate proportional to the amount present.' Which equation?

options.label: dA/dt = −kA
options.feedback: Right — proportional to the amount, and negative because it is LEAVING.

options.label: dA/dt = −k
options.feedback: That is a constant rate of loss, regardless of how much is there — which is not what 'proportional' means.
